strengths: The paper presents a complete, coherent framework for low-rank variational inference in BNNs, implemented from scratch for MLPs, LSTMs, and Transformers, with architecture-specific care (e.g., cached weight sampling for LSTMs per Fortunato et al., position-wise factorization for Transformers).

The Gaussian complexity transfer result (Section 3.5 / Appendix E) is the strongest technical contribution: the observation that the posterior predictive mean lies in the closed convex hull of the rank-r support class, combined with convex-hull and closure invariance of vector-valued Gaussian complexity, cleanly extends deterministic rank-sensitive bounds (Pinto et al., 2025) to Bayesian predictors. This is a genuinely nice, self-contained argument.

Empirical evaluation is broad (MIMIC-III, Beijing air quality, SST-2, MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, toy regression) with a consistent narrative of a calibration-OOD tradeoff, selective prediction gains, and parameter efficiency (up to 15x fewer parameters than Deep Ensembles).

The limitations discussion is unusually honest: the authors acknowledge that Gaussian complexity bounds are vacuous in practice, that training-time gains do not materialize at small scales, that confidence intervals overlap across seeds, and that comparisons with SWAG and low-rank covariance methods are missing.

Reproducibility is well supported: detailed hardware/software configuration, seeds, hyperparameter choices, KL annealing schedules, and rank-selection procedures are documented in Appendices F, G, and H.
weaknesses: The central 'singularity' claim (Theorem 3.4) is over-sold. That the pushforward of a distribution through W = AB^T is singular w.r.t. Lebesgue measure is an immediate consequence of any low-rank parameterization (including LoRA, rank-1 perturbations, subspace inference) and requires only standard measure theory. It does not distinguish this method from other low-rank approaches as strongly as the framing suggests.

The PAC-Bayes result (Theorem 3.8) is essentially a parameter-counting argument relying on the assumption of equal per-parameter KL bounds; the interesting question of whether the actual KL for low-rank posteriors is genuinely smaller is not established. The Gaussian complexity bounds are admittedly vacuous, so the theoretical 'provable benefits' claimed in the abstract are not supported by non-vacuous guarantees.

Theorems 3.6/3.7 compare a learned W to an unknown full-rank optimum W*; the decomposition into learning error ||W - W*_r||_F and rank bias is informative only if the full-rank optimum has fast singular value decay, which is validated only empirically on a handful of layers. The bounds are thus loose and somewhat circular as guidance.

Originality relative to prior Bayesian low-rank methods (Bayesian-LoRA of Yang et al. 2024, BLoB, BELLA, subspace inference, low-rank covariance VI) is incremental; the main differentiator is training from random initialization rather than any new variational family. The claim that 'no prior work trains low-rank BNNs end-to-end' is asserted but not rigorously substantiated.

Experimental scale is modest relative to the scalability claims: the largest model is a 9.9M-parameter BERT-mini-style transformer trained from scratch (SST-2 accuracy ~0.80, well below pre-trained-model baselines), and there is no comparison with SGLD, SWAG, or low-rank covariance methods (acknowledged). With only 4-5 seeds and overlapping intervals, several headline improvements (e.g., OOD detection over Deep Ensembles on MIMIC-III) are not statistically established.

Some presentation and consistency issues: Table 2 contains missing/placeholder entries for the deterministic baseline; numbers in the appendix occasionally differ from the main text (e.g., AUPR-OOD 0.81 in Figure 11 vs 0.788 in Table 1); the seeding of figures vs tables (5 seeds vs 4 runs) is inconsistent in places.

The initialization theory in Appendix F matches only second moments of the posterior mean of W and glosses over the fact that induced weight entries are correlated with each other and that sampling noise contributes additional variance, weakening the claimed 'principled' foundation.
